intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRB1 gene (137190) on chromosome 4p12.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is a neurologic disorder with onset of seizures in infancy. Reported patients have had epileptic encephalopathy presenting as infantile spasms or as epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS), with severe to profound developmental impairment and hypotonia. The disorder has been associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in GABRB1.

paragraphs.text: The Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) sequenced the exomes of 264 trios, each with a proband who had infantile spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. They found de novo mutations in GABA(A) receptor subunit genes in 6 patients: 4 in GABRB3, 1 in GABRA1, and 1 in GABRB1. The de novo GABRB1 mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of the proband and parents. The authors proposed that individual rare mutations in different genes may converge on a shared pathway. They also found a significant excess of de novo mutations in the roughly 4,000 genes most intolerant to functional genetic variation (p = 2.9 x 10(-3)), and estimated that about 90 intolerant genes may confer risk of epileptic encephalopathy.

paragraphs.text: Janve et al. (2016) functionally studied the de novo heterozygous GABRB1 mutation found by the Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013), a phe246-to-ser (F246S) substitution in transmembrane domain 1 at a residue that is invariant across all GABA-A receptor subunits. When the beta-1 F246S subunit was coexpressed with alpha-1 and gamma-2L subunits in HEK293T cells, peak GABA-evoked current density fell by only about 25% in the homozygous expression condition and was unchanged in the heterozygous condition. Current deactivation was markedly slowed; in single-channel recordings, mean open time increased about 3.75-fold and burst duration about 3.2-fold, while single-channel conductance fell to about 21 pS. The mutation increased holding currents about 5-fold in the homozygous expression condition, and these currents were partly blocked by zinc. In the absence of GABA, mutant receptors had a 4-fold higher spontaneous open probability, indicating spontaneous channel opening. Surface levels of the mutant subunit were slightly but significantly reduced, while total levels were unchanged. Despite the lack of an established link between GABRB1 and epilepsy syndromes, the authors concluded that their results suggested GABRB1 is a candidate human epilepsy gene.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with EIMFS from a cohort of 135 patients, Burgess et al. (2019) identified a de novo heterozygous missense variant in the GABRB1 gene (chr4:47405633T-C), resulting in an ile247-to-thr (I247T) substitution, by whole-exome sequencing. The variant was classified as likely pathogenic. GABRB1 had not previously been linked to EIMFS but had been reported in other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, and the authors used this finding to stress the role of GABA-related mechanisms in EIMFS.

paragraphs.text: Janve et al. (2016) observed that the mutations associated with infantile spasms (GABRB3 N110D and GABRB1 F246S) lay at beta-minus subunit interfaces and mainly changed current kinetics, whereas the mutations associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome lay at the beta-plus/alpha-minus interface and mainly reduced peak GABA-evoked currents. The authors cautioned that the contribution of these mutations to the epilepsy phenotype is difficult to judge from in vitro data alone.

paragraphs.text: Janve et al. (2016) proposed that the faster rise time and slower deactivation caused by the GABRB1 F246S mutation would lengthen the first inhibitory postsynaptic current. However, they suggested that it would reduce charge transfer during later currents by lowering the number of unbound receptors, especially during high-frequency firing, resulting in a net loss of GABAergic inhibition.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with epileptic encephalopathy from a cohort of probands with infantile spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, the Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) identified a de novo heterozygous mutation in the GABRB1 gene by exome sequencing of trios; the de novo status was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of the proband and parents. Janve et al.
